FXUS62 KRAH 111845
AFDRAH

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Raleigh NC
245 PM EDT Fri Sep 11 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...

* Minor PoP adjustments for this weekend, otherwise no major changes.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 245 PM Friday...

1) Unsettled wx pattern this weekend, potentially wet at times later 
Saturday. 

2) Mainly dry with temps closer to seasonable values much of next 
week. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 245 PM Friday...

1) Unsettled wx pattern this weekend, potentially wet at times later 
Saturday. 

An upper short wave trough currently moving across the Miss Valley 
will lift NE across the TN Valley tomorrow and exit off the Mid-
Atlantic coast by mid-day Sunday.  In response, we'll see several 
opportunities for showers and tstms through early Sunday, the first 
of which being widely scattered showers and tstms the rest of today, 
a few of which could include an isolated strong or possibly damaging 
wind gust (see SWODY1 for additional details).  

Saturday, particularly later in the day and early night, appears to 
be the most unsettled part of the weekend as the trough approaches 
and begins moving across. While a shower/tstm will be possible any 
time Saturday, the most likely time and best coverage will likely be 
late in the day from mid-afternoon hours through the late evening 
hours. It's worth noting that central NC is included in the Days 1 
and 2 ERO, so any of the heavier downpours could results in isold 
flooding of the typical spots that are more sensitive to heavy 
downpours, such as urban and low-lying areas. 

While the bulk of the prefrontal shower/tstm activity should be to 
our east by daybreak Sunday morning, we can't rule out a few 
additional showers or tstms assoc with the actual frontal passage 
which will occur later Sunday, thus the reason for the ongoing 
elevated PoPs Sunday afternoon; however, coverage and intensity 
should be much less compared to the previous day.  

2) Mainly dry with temps closer to seasonable values much of next 
week.  

Most of next week will be dry thanks to an upper ridge that will be 
positioned to our west much of the time and resulting dry northerly 
flow. In addition, the airmass... while still a few deg above 
normal... will at least be closer to normal with highs each day 
generally in the 80s.  It's worth noting that a closed upper trough, 
broken off from a larger-scale trough moving off the Northeast 
states early next week, will drift south parallel to the East Coast. 
 Today's NWP models forecast it to remain far enough offshore so 
that our only impact from it will be occasional gusty NE winds at 
times during the mid-week period. 

&&

.AVIATION /18Z FRIDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/... 
As of 245 PM Friday...

The rest of this afternoon and evening should remain generally VFR 
at most if not all sites. A brief shower or thunderstorm may be 
possible at any site this evening, however any cells that have tried 
to develop over the area thus far have not lasted long before 
dissipating. If a cell does sustain and track over the airport, 
there could be lightning and/or gusty winds. Tonight, there is 
expected to be low stratus/fog over much or all of central NC, 
bringing the chance of IFR to LIFR ceilings and/or visibilities to 
all TAF sites. The Triad (INT/GSO) terminals look like they could 
remain MVFR into the afternoon, while the rest of the terminals 
should return to VFR. Saturday afternoon should have a greater 
chance of rain impacting terminals, however should hold off until 
around or after 18Z. 

Outlook: Shower and thunderstorm chances will continue through 
Saturday evening as a cold front makes its way through central NC.
Low stratus and/or fog may develop and cause sub-VFR restrictions 
again the Sunday and Monday mornings as well. 

&&

.RAH WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$

FXUS62 KILM 111823
AFDILM

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Wilmington NC
223 PM EDT Fri Sep 11 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
Forecast rain chances have been reduced by 10-20 percent for
both Saturday and Sunday, but the likelihood for isolated heavy
rainfall amounts still continues. Forecast low temperatures for
Tuesday night and Wednesday night have been adjusted downward 
2-3 degrees.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
1) Deep Gulf moisture and a break in the ridge aloft will 
maintain good chances for showers and thunderstorms through 
Sunday.

2) Well-above normal temperatures and high humidity will 
maintain daytime heat indices at or above 100 degrees through 
Monday.

3) A modified Canadian airmass should bring near-normal 
temperatures beginning Tuesday.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Deep Gulf moisture and a break in the ridge aloft will 
maintain good chances for showers and thunderstorms through 
Sunday.

This morning's 12z CHS weather balloon measured a precipitable 
water of 2.35 inches. That's one-third of an inch above the 90th
climatological percentile and near the daily max for this time 
of year. Deep Gulf moisture will continue to stream northeastward
across the eastern Carolinas through Sunday morning between a 
mid level ridge east of the Bahamas and a trough over the Mid-
Mississippi Valley.

Surface-based CAPE near 2000 J/kg, forecast 0-6 km bulk shear
around 10 knots, and little-to-no dry air aloft argues for
single-cell storm development on Saturday with heavy rain 
potential. Some loose storm organization could occur along the 
seabreeze front and any outflow boundaries, but severe weather 
risk should remain very low. HREF ensemble 24-hr max precip of 
3-5 inches implies there will be a few isolated heavy totals 
within the sea of 0.25 to 0.50 inch weekend amounts.

The upper trough producing the break in the ridge should slide 
eastward across the Carolinas on Sunday, perhaps enhancing bulk
shear to around 20 knots. Multicells should become possible, 
perhaps bringing better potential for gusty winds. The upper 
trough should shift offshore Sunday night ahead of rising mid 
and upper level heights spreading eastward from the Mid South.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Well-above normal temperatures and high humidity will 
maintain daytime heat indices at or above 100 degrees through 
Monday.

850 mb temps in the +18C to +19C range should continue through
the weekend. This is at or above the 90th climatological 
percentile for mid September. If it weren't for the increased 
cloudiness and convection expected this weekend we'd probably be
looking at Heat Advisory-level conditions. 

As it stands now, forecast highs in the upper 80s to around 90 
coupled with dewpoints well into the 70s should yield heat 
indices in the 100-103 range through Monday.

NWS ILM has never issued a Heat Advisory later than September 5
since the introduction of VTEC product codes twenty years ago.
(and that latest advisory was earlier this month)


KEY MESSAGE 3...A modified Canadian airmass should bring near-normal 
temperatures beginning Tuesday.

Models have all come into line over the past 24 hours showing
the strongest Canadian high we've seen since last Spring moving
across New England Tuesday into Wednesday. This should push a
cold front southward across the eastern Carolinas Monday night,
allowing a modified Canadian airmass to spread across the area
Tuesday into Wednesday. This won't be crisp, dry Canadian air by
any means given its long passage across water temps in the 70s 
and 80s, but it should bring cooler air across the area knocking
temperatures back down closer to normal for mid September.

Forecast lows in particular look refreshing with 60s expected
for all but east-facing beaches Tuesday night and Wednesday
night. Some inland locations could conceivably dip to 60
degrees.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z FRIDAY THROUGH WEDNESDAY/...
Dense tropical moisture streaming across the Carolinas should
yield scattered showers and thunderstorms this afternoon.
Coverage should be greatest in the vicinity of the seabreeze
front near or just west of KCRE and KMYR through 21z. Scattered
showers and storms inland will develop in loose clusters moving
northeastward with the mid level winds. All of this convective
activity will be accompanied by brief MVFR/IFR conditions, and 
should tend to dissipate this evening with the loss of 
sunlight.

Late tonight there is a moderate potential for LIFR ceilings to
develop over KFLO and KLBT mainly after 10z, lingering through
13-14z much like we saw this morning. These low stratus clouds
should lift into a cumulus cloud deck with bases 2500-3500 feet
AGL after 14-15z Saturday with another round of showers and 
thunderstorms anticipated to develop during the heat of the day.

Extended Outlook...Scattered showers and thunderstorms bringing
brief MVFR/IFR conditions are expected Saturday afternoon and
again Sunday afternoon. There is also a low potential for late 
night/early morning stratus or ground fog affecting KLBT and 
KFLO late Saturday night and again late Sunday night. VFR
conditions should prevail Monday through Wednesday as a more
stable and drier Canadian airmass builds in from the northeast.

&&

.MARINE...
Tonight through Tuesday night...Models continue to consistently
show a cold front stalling across interior North Carolina 
tonight, then lifting back north on Saturday with no direct 
impact on our weather or winds this far south. Light to moderate
southwesterly winds are expected to continue through the 
weekend along with multiple waves of showers and thunderstorms 
Saturday through Sunday night. 

Drier weather should develop on Monday as high pressure
strengthens aloft over the Carolinas. The strongest Canadian
high we've seen since last Spring should move across New England
Tuesday and Wednesday, pushing a cold front southward across the
Carolina coastal waters Monday night. Northeast winds behind the
front should increase to a solid 20 knots offshore and 15-20 
knots nearshore Tuesday into Tuesday night. Seas within 20 
miles of shore could build to 4-6 feet with dominant wave
periods near 6 seconds.

&&

.ILM WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
NC...Coastal Flood Advisory from 9 PM this evening to 1 AM EDT 
     Saturday for NCZ107.
SC...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

WHAT HAS CHANGED...TRA
KEY MESSAGES...TRA
DISCUSSION...TRA
AVIATION...TRA
MARINE...TRA

000
FXUS62 KJAX 111833
AFDJAX

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Jacksonville FL
233 PM EDT Fri Sep 11 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

For the latest NE FL and SE GA Daily Key Messages please visit:
https:/www.weather.gov/media/jax/briefings/nws-jax-briefing.pdf

- Numerous Afternoon and Evening Thunderstorms Expected through
  Saturday. Strong Storm Potential Along the I-95 Corridor  
  During the Late Afternoon Hours. Stronger Storms May Produce 
  Wind Gusts of 40-55 mph, Frequent Lightning Strikes, and 
  Torrential Downpours that Could Result in Localized Flooding.

- Daily Peak Heat Index Values of 104-108 Degrees Expected 
  through Monday.

- Scattered Afternoon and Evening Thunderstorms Are Expected
  from Sunday through Wednesday.

- Moderate Rip Current Risk Continues at All Area Beaches
  through Monday. High Risk Likely from Tuesday through Thursday 
  as Breezy Onshore Winds Develop at Coastal Locations. 

&&

.NEAR TERM /THROUGH TONIGHT/...
Main Highlights:

- Numerous Afternoon and Evening Thunderstorms Today. Strong 
  Storm Potential Along the I-95 Corridor During the Late 
  Afternoon Hours. Stronger Storms May Produce Wind Gusts of 
  40-55 mph, Frequent Lightning Strikes, and Torrential 
  Downpours that Could Result in Localized Flooding.

- Moderate Rip Current Risk Continues at All Area Beaches. 

Afternoon surface analysis depicts weakening Atlantic high
pressure  (1019 millibars) situated off the southeastern 
seaboard, with this feature extending its axis westward across 
north central FL. Meanwhile, a frontal boundary stretching from 
North Carolina's Outer Banks westward across the Tennessee 
Valley and the Ozarks was in the process of stalling as another 
weak high pressure center stretches across the Great Lakes, Mid-
Atlantic states and New England in the wake of this boundary. 
Aloft...deep-layered ridging was centered just northeast of the 
Bahamas, which was directing a shortwave trough located on the 
western periphery of this feature north- northeastward across 
western portions of the FL panhandle. Otherwise, a potent 
shortwave trough was digging eastward across the Ozarks towards 
the Tennessee Valley. Latest GOES-East derived Total 
Precipitable Water imagery indicates that deep tropical moisture
remains in place area-wide, with PWAT values generally in the 2
- 2.3 inch range across our area. Convection on the leading 
edge of the shortwave trough that was crossing western portions 
of the FL panhandle has crossed the Alapaha and Suwannee Rivers,
with only isolated showers located elsewhere, mainly at inland 
locations. Temperatures at 18Z were generally in the upper 80s 
and lower 90s, with dewpoints mostly in the low to mid 70s 
creating heat index values mostly around 100. 

Abundant tropical moisture and continued slow cooling of
temperatures aloft should allow for showers and thunderstorms 
to become numerous across our region as the afternoon 
progresses, with southwesterly steering flow bringing convection
towards the I-95 corridor late this afternoon, where activity 
could linger into the early evening hours. The presence of a 
pinned Atlantic sea breeze boundary along the I-95 corridor and 
other mesoscale boundary collisions should allow for storms to 
"pulse" and potentially become strong later this afternoon, 
especially as convection intersects the Atlantic sea breeze 
boundary that should be positioned near I-95. Storms that pulse 
and become strong will be capable of producing downburst winds 
of 40-50 mph, along with frequent lightning strikes and 
torrential downpours. Given the deep tropical moisture in place,
any storms that "back-build" along mesoscale boundaries such as
the Atlantic sea breeze could result in localized flooding, 
especially if this potential event occurs at urban or low-lying,
normally flood prone locations. 

Convection could linger into the early to mid evening hours
tonight, especially along the I-95 corridor in southeast GA, 
where convection may not arrive until later this afternoon. 
Otherwise, debris cloud cover will thin out after midnight, with
deepening southwesterly flow likely developing a greater 
coverage of predawn convection over Apalachee Bay than what was 
observed this morning. Some of this activity could move onshore 
along the FL Big Bend and Nature Coasts towards sunrise, but 
activity should remain west of the Suwannee River and north 
central FL through the early morning hours on Saturday. Lows 
will fall to the low and mid 70s across most of our area.

&&

.SHORT TERM /SATURDAY THROUGH SUNDAY NIGHT/...

Main Highlights This Period:

- Potential for isolated strong thunderstorms and localized
  flooding on Saturday.

Southwest steering flow continues to bring in enhanced moisture 
(PWATs 2.2-2.4") across the area, prompting numerous showers and
storms Saturday afternoon and evening. The Gulf sea breeze will
push further inland, meeting the Atlantic sea breeze closer to 
the east coast/I-95 corridor, which is where our best chance for
strong thunderstorm development will be. Gusty winds will be 
the primary threat with any strong storms, but also heavy 
rainfall may cause localized flooding concerns, especially in 
urban and typically flood prone areas. High temperatures 
Saturday will be in the low 90s, with max afternoon heat index 
values peaking around 104-107 for portions of northeast Florida.

Convection is expected to be less widespread on Sunday as the
high pressure ridge shifts northward and crosses over the 
forecast area, with the prevailing flow gradually shifting to a 
more northeasterly onshore flow by the beginning of next week. 
Overall, precipitation chances will be about 20-40% across much 
of the area, with higher chances over north central Florida. 
Similar high temperatures are expected Sunday, in the lower 90s.

&&

.LONG TERM /MONDAY THROUGH FRIDAY/...

Main Highlights This Period Monday through Thursday: 

- Daily Thunderstorm Potential Each Day Next Week.

- High Rip Current Risk Likely at All Area Beaches from Tuesday
  through Thursday as Breezy Onshore Winds Develop at Coastal
  Locations. 

Northwesterly flow Monday gradually shifts to northeasterly 
Tuesday, beginning a few day period of stronger onshore flow 
through Thursday. Tuesday through Thursday, those breezy 
easterly surface winds will bring showers and isolated 
thunderstorms onshore in the mornings, with coverage expanding 
inland throughout the day. For daily afternoon and evening 
storms, the focus will be generally south of I-10 each day. High
temperatures gradually lower throughout the week, Monday highs 
will be in the lower to mid 90s, and by Thursday areas closer to
the east coast will peak in the mid 80s.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z FRIDAY THROUGH 18Z SATURDAY/...

VFR conditions will prevail at the regional terminals through at 
least 19Z. Showers and thunderstorms will begin developing near 
the regional terminals towards 19Z, with TEMPO groups for brief 
surface wind gusts up to 25 knots and IFR conditions during 
heavier downpours used through around 00Z. Convection may linger
at the Duval County terminals, SGJ, and SSI through around 03Z 
this evening, where PROB30 groups for brief surface wind gusts 
up to 25 knots and IFR visibilities during heavier downpours 
were used during the evening hours. VFR conditions should then 
prevail at the regional terminals before 04Z Saturday. MVFR to 
IFR visibilities are then likely to develop at VQQ after 07Z, 
with confidence only high enough to forecast prevailing MVFR 
visibilities at this time. Low MVFR ceilings of 1,000 - 2,000 
feet are then forecast to develop at the SSI and SGJ coastal 
terminals towards 14Z Saturday.

&&

.MARINE...

Weakening high pressure situated off the southeastern seaboard
will continue to shift southward as a frontal boundary stalls 
across the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas. The axis of this 
feature will remain south of our local waters through the 
weekend, resulting in prevailing south to southwest winds, with 
the afternoon sea breeze providing onshore winds for the near 
shore waters. Thunderstorms will likely develop over coastal 
locations during the mid to late afternoon hours that will 
generally progress eastward across our local waters during the 
late afternoon and evening hours through the weekend, with a few
stronger storms containing strong wind gusts, frequent 
lightning strikes, and torrential downpours possible each 
afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, high pressure strengthening 
over the Great Lakes region in the wake of a cold front on 
Sunday and Monday will wedge down the southeastern seaboard by 
Tuesday and Wednesday. Onshore winds will develop across our 
local waters on Monday night, followed by northeasterly winds 
strengthening on Tuesday and especially Tuesday night and 
Wednesday, when a period of Small Craft Advisory conditions will
be possible, accompanied by building seas that will likely 
persist through Thursday.

Rip Currents: Offshore winds during the morning hours through  
Monday will tend to reduce the rip current risk at area beaches.
The afternoon sea breeze will create breakers of 2-3 feet at 
the northeast FL beaches, which will combine with a lingering 
easterly ocean swell to create a lower end moderate risk, 
especially during the outgoing tide. Breakers of only 1-2 feet 
at the southeast GA beaches will likely yield a low risk through
Monday. Northeasterly winds will develop on Monday night and 
will likely become breezy on Tuesday, likely resulting in a high
risk at all area beaches from the afternoon hours through at 
least Thursday as breakers build.

&&

.FIRE WEATHER...

Diurnal southwesterly winds will persist through the end of the
week and through the weekend. As a result of the moist 
southwesterly flow, the diurnal east coast sea breeze will be 
pinned near the shoreline and not reach inland much past the 
I-95 corridor. Flow pattern is expected to shift to become more 
onshore by the beginning of next week.

Fog Potential: Gusty and erratic wind shifts will occur from  
thunderstorm activity. Patchy fog is expected across inland areas 
the next couple of mornings, with widespread dense fog unlikely.

&&


.PRELIMINARY POINT TEMPS/POPS...
AMG  72  92  73  92 /  30  40  20  20 
SSI  75  90  77  91 /  60  40  20  30 
JAX  73  92  74  92 /  60  70  30  40 
SGJ  75  90  75  91 /  50  60  20  40 
GNV  73  92  73  91 /  40  70  20  40 
OCF  73  92  74  92 /  50  70  40  70 

&&

.JAX WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
FL...None.
GA...None.
MARINE...None.

&&

$$

000
FXUS65 KBOU 111808
AFDBOU

Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Denver/Boulder CO
1208 PM MDT Fri Sep 11 2026

.KEY MESSAGES...

- Very warm today with only isolated high based showers/virga 
  late this afternoon and evening.

- Slight increase in shower/storm coverage this weekend. Cooler
  Saturday, then warmer Sunday.

- Unsettled pattern next week, with multiple cold fronts expected
  to bring a few more noticeable cooldowns.

&&

.DISCUSSION /Through Thursday/...
Issued at 231 AM MDT Fri Sep 11 2026

Zonal flow aloft will strengthen today, bringing a stronger
downslope component and thus a bit more warming. We expect highs 
to reach 90F or more over most of the plains and I-25 Corridor. 
To offset that, there is some mid/upper level moisture evident on 
satellite and radar now reaching northern Utah. This will continue
to push east today, resulting in enough for scattered virga,
isolated high based showers, and even a lone weak storm. The main
threat of any light precipitation would be over the northern 
mountains this afternoon, spreading to the northern plains this 
evening, but even there coverage would be sparse. Any high based 
showers/virga would support gusty outflow winds to 40 mph given 
increasing environmental flow and DCAPE increasing to 800-1200 
J/kg. 

For tonight, a cold front pushes south across the High Plains and
through northeast Colorado late tonight into early Saturday
morning. This will lead to cooler temperatures (near normal) for
Saturday. While moisture levels increase slightly, considerable
uncertainty exists for afternoon and evening shower/storm coverage
due to thermal profiles. For the most part, we don't think we'll
reach convective temps over the plains but still can't rule out
a few late day showers and storms spilling eastward from the
higher terrain due to mid level instability and moisture. 

Sunday will likely feature a return to much above normal
temperatures. MOS guidance suggest highs pushing into the mid 90s
for metro Denver and the I-25 Urban Corridor. That may be a bit
aggressive as there is some guidance (not surprisingly) slowing 
the redevelopment of lee troughing and erosion of low level
moisture. The record for Denver on the 13th is 96F set in 2018, 
1990, and 1895, but at this point it appears we'll most likely 
stay a couple degrees shy of that. With regard to convection, 
isolated showers and storms will be high based and relatively 
weak. However, if a storm or two can break the cap over the 
northeast plains they could certainly tap into higher MLCAPE and 
become severe. 

As discussed yesterday, the cooldown for Monday appears to be
tempered as the next cold front/upper trough has been delayed 
slightly. However, there is still high confidence in more 
significant cooling for Tuesday behind a moderately strong early 
(meteorological) autumn cold front. While daily uncertainties 
exist about the degree of cooling, there is modest agreement we'll
settle into highs in the 70s (and 30-40% chance of 60s) for the 
plains and I-25 Corridor. A brief warmup is possible for 
Wednesday before yet another front arrives Thursday. Ensembles are
in decent agreement holding a plume of mid/upper level moisture 
and higher than normal climatological precipitable water over us.
Thus, we should have daily chances of showers and storms most of 
the days this upcoming week. 

&&

.AVIATION /18Z TAFS through 18Z Saturday/...
Issued at 1206 PM MDT Fri Sep 11 2026

VFR expected through the TAF period. Winds over the region are 
currently light (<10KT) and NW/N, with the exception of a channel of 
stronger downsloping WNW winds near KBJC occasionally gusting up to 
20KT. We expect northwesterly flow to prevail this afternoon through 
sunset (01Z-02Z). There is a chance for high-based showers to take 
shape late this afternoon although coverage is expected to be 
sparse. Nevertheless, dry microbursts and outflows could lead to 
erratic winds gusting up to 35KT near the showers. 

Winds tonight are a bit uncertain although there will likely be a 
return to SW/S drainage flow by 04Z. A cold frontal passage will 
bring a northerly wind shift ~10Z. 

&&

.BOU WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
None.

&&

$$
